We can, however, show that the region can be divided into a finite number of sub-regions for each of which the condition <math>(z, z_0)</math>, above, is satisfied for all points <math>z</math>, within or upon the boundary of this sub-region, for an appropriate position of <math>z_0</math>, within or upon the boundary of this sub-region. Hence it can be proved that, for a differentiable function <math>f(z)</math>, the integral <math>\int_{z_1}^{z} f(z)dz</math> has the same value by whatever path within the region we pass from <math>z_1</math> to <math>z</math>. Consider first a triangle over which the condition <math>(z, z_0)</math> holds, for some position of <math>z_0</math> and every position of <math>z</math>, within or upon the boundary of the triangle. Two remarks should be added: (1) The theorem is proved only on condition that the closed path of integration belongs to the region at every point of which the conditions are satisfied. (2) The theorem, though proved only when the region consists of triangles, holds also when the boundary points of the region consist of one or more closed paths, no two of which meet.

Hence we can deduce the remarkable result that the value of <math>f(z)</math> at any interior point of a region is expressible in terms of the value of <math>f(z)</math> at the boundary points. § 5. ''Applications''.—The previous results have manifold applications.

(1) If an infinite series of differentiable functions of <math>z</math> be uniformly convergent along a certain path lying with the region of definition of the functions, so that <math>\text{S}(z) = u_0(z) + u_1(z) + \dots + u_{n-1}(z) + \text{R}_n(z)</math>, where <math>|\text{R}_n(z)| < \epsilon</math> for all points of the path, we have

{{block center|<math>\int_{z_0}^z\text{S}(z)dz = \int_{z_0}^z u_0(z)dz + \int_{z_0}^z u_1(z)dz + \dots + \int_{z_0}^z u_{n-1}(z)dz + \int_{z_0}^z\text{R}_n(z)dz</math>,}}

wherein, in absolute value, <math>\int_{z_0}^z\text{R}_n(z)dz < \epsilon\text{L}</math>, if <math>\text{L}</math> be the length of the path. Thus the series may be integrated, and the resulting series is also uniformly convergent.

About every interior point <math>z_0</math> of the region of existence the function may be represented by a power series in <math>z-z_0</math>, and the series converges and represents the function over any circle centre at <math>z_0</math> which contains no singular point in its interior. This has been proved above. And it can be similarly proved, putting <math>z=1/\zeta</math>, that if the region of existence of the function contains all points of the plane for which <math>|z|>\text{R}</math>, then the function is representable for all such points by a power series in <math>z^{-1}</math> or <math>\zeta</math>; in such case we say that the region of existence of the function contains the point <math>z=\infty</math>. A series in <math>z^{-1}</math> has a finite limit when <math>|z|=\infty</math>; a series in <math>z</math> cannot remain finite for all points <math>z</math> for which <math>|z|>\text{R}</math>; for if, for <math>|z|=\text{R}</math>, the sum of a power series <math>\Sigma a_nz^n</math> in <math>z</math> is in absolute value less than <math>\text{M}</math>, we have <math>|a_n|<\text{M}r^{-n}</math>, and therefore, if <math>\text{M}</math> remains finite for all values of <math>r</math> however great, <math>a_n=0</math>. Thus the region of existence of a function if it contains all finite points of the plane cannot contain the point <math>z=\infty</math>; such is, for instance, the case of the function <math>\text{exp}\ (z)=\Sigma z^n/n!</math>. This may be regarded as a particular case of a well-known result (§ 7), that the circumference of convergence of any power series representing the function contains at least one singular point. As an extreme case functions exist whose region of existence is circular, there being a singular point in every arc of the circumference, however small; for instance, this is the case for the functions represented for <math>|z|<1</math> by the series <math>\sum_{n=0} z^m</math>, where <math>m=n^2</math>, the series <math>\sum_{n=0} z^m</math> where <math>m=n!</math>, and the series <math>\sum_{n=1} z^m/(m+1)(m+2)</math> where <math>m=a^n</math>,

If <math>z_0</math> be a point interior to the circle of convergence of a series representing the function, the series may be rearranged in powers of <math>z - z_0</math>; as <math>z_0</math> approaches to a singular point of the function, lying on the circle of convergence, the radii of convergence of these derived series in <math>z - z_0</math> diminish to zero; when, however, a circle can be put about <math>z_0</math>, not containing any singular point of the function, but containing points outside the circle of convergence of the original series, then the series in <math>z - z_0</math> gives the value of the function for these external points. If the function be supposed to be given only for the interior of the original circle, by the original power series, the series in <math>z - z_0</math> converging beyond the original circle gives what is known as an ''analytical continuation'' of the function.
